subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, May 7, consideration in committee of a resolution to provide sums not exceeding $2,000,000,000 for the year ending March 31, 1943, for granting to his majesty aid for national defence and security-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.

Hon. ANGUS L. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services): Yesterday there were some questions asked the answers to which I promised to endeavour to bring down to-day. I have some at least of the answers here.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) asked whether cadet training was uniform in the three services-that was the gist of his question. I have here the syllabus of training issued under the direction of the chief of the general staff. It gives the subjects that are common to the army and air force cadets, and they constitute the great bulk of the subjects. There are a few subjects which are taken by air cadets and not by army cadets, and vice versa. For instance, I find that air cadets give nine hours' study to air frames; naturally the army gives no time to that subject. On the other hand the army gives twenty hours to small arms training, as against only six hours for the air force, and so on. The syllabus of training prepared for the use of sea cadets is considerably different, and I think inevitably so. I find for instance that sea cadets are required to study seamanship, how to sling and lash a hammock, how to lay out bedding, et cetera; the meaning of naval terms, customs of the naval service, bends and hitches, knotting and splicing, rules of the road at sea, the use of the compass and the helm, the use of the lead and line, anchors and cables, and the like. So that there is a great difference between the training of sea cadets and the training of army or air cadets; and on reflection I think it will be seen that it is impossible to have uniformity of training in these three branches as far as cadets are concerned.
Another question asked by several hon. members was in regard to naval pay and allowances. I intimated some time last week that the matter was under consideration by the treasury board, and I think I said again last night that I had been before the treasury board several times, that they were considering the question and were on the point of reaching a decision. I am very happy to announce now that that decision has been

War Appropriation-Naval Services
reached, and that from April 1 of this year the dependents' allowances granted to wives and children of men in the naval service will be on a parity with those granted to wives and children of men in the army and air force.
So that it would appear that all the criticism directed against the navy in that connection was well founded.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I would not say it has been entirely well founded. The navy was better off in some respects than the army, and not so well off in others. We shall have to lower from now on the amount granted to men out of quarters, which will bring it more into line with the army and the air force, and one or two other little adjustments will have to be made. But I think that the present arrangement is, as a whole, more equitable than the former one.
The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) asked whether dependents of men in the navy could draw from the war allowances adjustment fund. The answer is yes, they can do so in the same way as the dependents of members of the other armed forces.
A somewhat similar question was asked by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), who put this case: if an ex-army man is in receipt of veteran's allowance and his son joins the navy and gives the father some assigned pay, is the veteran's allowance diminished to the extent of the assigned pay. I am instructed by Colonel Marriott, the secretary of the war veterans' allowance board, that that would not be the case unless the total received by the veteran from the veterans' allowance board and from the son were more than $60 a month. So long as it remains under $60 the veterans' allowance board will not in any way reduce the original grant.
Questions were asked by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and other hon. members with regard to convoys, and I asked that I be given some little time to think over that matter. I have done so, in such time as I have had at my disposal to-day, and I can say first of all that the losses to ships in convoy are generally much less than those to ships out of convoy. I am not speaking of any given day, but taking a period such as a year, we estimate that the losses to ships in convoy run something like one-quarter of the losses to ships out of convoy. The losses on the north Atlantic, the east-west route from these shores to Great Britain, since the beginning of the 
war, in convoyed ships, still runs less than 1 per cent. I need not give the exact figure, but it is less than 1 per cent for the period of two and a half years. In other words less than 1 per cent of the ships setting out from these shores in convoy have been sunk by enemy action.
What is the ratio having regard to the early period of the war and the present period?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman mean are the sinkings more serious?
Yes, that is really what I mean.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I should say that on the east-west route, the ordinary route from this country to Great Britain, the sinkings are not unusually alarming at this time. I do not think they are out of the ordinary. There are heavy sinkings, of course, on the north-south route, as I intimated last night.

That is
where there are no convoys?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes. The sinkings there are very heavy, but the percentage I gave previously is about right even for that route. Ships travelling out of convoy and subjected to enemy action we think are four times as vulnerable, or perhaps even more, as ships travelling in convoy.
The Canadian navy does the convoying?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The convoying from here to Britain is done in part by the Canadian navy, in part by the British navy and in part by the United States navy, with the three sharing in about equal measure. Certain sections, of course, are exclusively under the control of the Canadian navy.	.

I am sure we were all gratified by the announcement made by the minister that adjustments are to be made in the allowances given seamen and their dependents. I wonder if the minister would place the amended scale of allowances on Hansard, so that they may be available to all hon. members. When this matter first came up some days ago and I suggested that some adjustment should be made I stated to the Minister of National Defence, whose department was under consideration at the time, that in my opinion the whole matter of the uniformity of dependents' allowances and pay in the various services might well

War Appropriation-Naval Services
be gone into. I offer that suggestion to the minister again at this time. Instead of having to equalize rates of pay by means of various amounts payable for subsistence allowances when men are out of barracks, and that sort of thing, the straight rates of pay should be more nearly equal, and the dependents' allowances should be more nearly equal, so that the confusion which now exists in the minds of the public and of the men in the services may be removed, and further so that if the administration should grant the cost of living bonus, which has been so strongly urged by all hon. members of this house, that bonus may be more easily applied, without creating additional confusion.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I could not produce at the moment a table showing the new scales of pay, but perhaps the house would permit me to place it on record on Monday.

Put it in the Votes and
Proceedings.
Mr. MACDONALD	(Kingston City):
Very well. It takes a little time to prepare a new table for all ranks, and the work can only be undertaken to-day.

Perhaps the minister would place it on Hansard on Monday, so that it may be generally available. The public do not get the Votes and Proceedings, as a rule.
Mr.	MACDONALD	(Kingston	City):
Very well.

I should like to mention a matter that has not been touched upon as yet. When the subcommittee of the war expenditures committee investigated the methods of handling stores in the various defence departments last summer, we were impressed with the efficiency of the method used by the naval branch. I believe we mentioned that in the report which we submitted to parliament last November. We spent a day in Halifax, where we saw the system in actual operation and had an opportunity of speaking to the men engaged in looking after the stores. I think we all realized that the responsibility of the man in charge of the warehouse containing the stores was very great indeed. Not only did he have several hundred thousand dollars worth of supplies to look after and distribute, but under his care was some of the most confidential and secret apparatus used by the navy. I need not say more about that. But we were astounded to find that the permanent civil servant in charge of those valuable stores and that secret equipment was
receiving, I believe, $1,320 a year; and at the time we were there, because for some reason he had been overpaid previously, a deduction of $10 a month was being made from his salary in order to make up that overpayment. This civil servant is a married man with a family, living in Halifax; and, as the minister said the other evening when we were discussing the question of pay, Halifax is not a city in which living is at all inexpensive. We found it difficult to understand why a man in charge of such valuable equipment should be receiving a salary altogether incommensurate with the responsibility which he had to assume. Indeed, we were astonished to find that this civil servant, in that responsible position, was actually receiving less than the men who were doing ordinary, common labour in the warehouse, moving the stores about. Up to the time we presented the report, I understand nothing had been done to rectify the situation. Has the matter been further considered, and has some salary more nearly commensurate with the responsibility been granted to the man in charge of stores at Halifax?
Could the hon. member say whether or not the man paid rent?
Yes; he was a married man with a family, living away from the warehouse, renting his own house.
He was not furnished with housing?
No.

I should like to support the representations of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar in regard to this matter. I am familiar with the work of the individual mentioned. His name has not been stated, but if he is the man in charge of the stores, I believe he is the same person I have in mind. If I remember correctly, the salary he is receiving is $1,440 and, as has already been stated, he has in his charge many hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of goods. He has been in the employ of the government for a period of about twenty-five years. I am glad to say that since the visit of that committee, to Halifax, not because of their representations but because of representations by others, this has been rectified to some extent and that official is now receiving $1,620. I still feel, however, that because of his responsibilities, and because of the efficient manner in which he is conducting his duty, he is far from receiving what he would receive if employed by a private firm in Halifax or any other city.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
I wish to pay a word of tribute to the efficient manner in -which contracts for stores in general have been administered in the naval dockyard at Halifax. For many years I was closely connected with that work, and was in a position to see the manner in which contracts were let and tenders received. I do not hesitate to say, as I have said to the minister on one occasion, that I cannot see any advantage, so far as the dockyard authorities at Halifax are concerned, in taking away their duties as purchasing and contract agents.
I am very happy to support the suggestion of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that an inquiry be instituted whereby not only that official but many other permanent officials in Halifax may be brought up to salaries in keeping with their duties. In this particular instance two persons were brought into Halifax at greatly increased salaries to carry on the duties of this one official. It was found, however, after a certain period of time that notwithstanding their qualifications and increased salaries they were unable to. carry out the duties in as efficient a manner as this permanent official had done. He is now carrying on that work, and I feel in fairness to him that he should receive at least the remuneration of the men from Montreal who were unable to carry out, or apparently did not carry out those duties in as efficient a manner as the present official.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Is that Mr. Pitman?
He is one who is underpaid, and Mr. McNamara is another. I believe the party the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar had in mind was Mr. "Jock" Matthews.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: A. A. Matthews?
No; I believe it is A. J. Matthews.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is likely the same man.
I had forgotten what the name was.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have the name of Matthews, but he is down as a clerk, grade 4.
The man I had in mind was in charge of the entire main stores at Halifax.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The naval stores officer there is Mr. Pitman. He receives a good deal more than the amount mentioned. I believe the amount he now receives is $2,760.
I do not think that is the man.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Mr. Pitman is receiving that amount now. However, some of those men were undoubtedly underpaid last year, and we have succeeded in getting some adjustments for many of them. This man may have been one.

There are on record not one but several letters dealing with the dockyards, and I am sure it will be found that
representations have been made not on behalf of one but of several who I consider are being underpaid.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The hon. member is quite right. He has several times brought this matter to my attention and to the attention, I believe, of the civil service commission. But he knows the problem that has arisen there. It is the old story between the permanent employee, who must advance along a regular scale, on the one hand, and the temporary employee, who comes in only for the duration of the war, on the other. The permanent employee gets certain advantages by way of pension, and the like, which the temporary employee does not get. He also has the advantage of security as long as he does his work. But there have been some glaring cases where men in permanent positions were called on to do work greatly in excess of what they would normally do, and we have adjusted some of those cases. If I had the name of the particular person-
I believe the name was Pitman.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: He is the stores officer, and is now receiving a salary of $2,760. So he is better off than he was last summer.

In view
of something said by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) about changing conditions with respect to stores at Halifax, the bringing in of a man from Montreal and the interposition of the Department of Munitions and Supply, would the minister tell us what the position. now is? Has there been a change in the modus operandi? Does the Department of Munitions and Supply now do the buying and the receiving? What is the inefficiency hinted at by the hon. member for Halifax?

Oh, no; pardon me-

War Appropriation-Naval Services

I may
have misconstrued the word used; I thought there was a reference to inefficiency or less efficiency.

I did not hint at any inefficiency, as far as the stores department at Halifax is concerned. Rather do I point out that there was no inefficiency, and I could not understand the change from the purchasing plan which formerly existed to that which is now conducted by the Department of Munitions and Supply.
They do the purchasing now?
Yes.

Yesterday the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), as reported at page 2236 of Hansard, made rather extended remarks with regard to what he considered as confusion with respect to the handling of seamen of the merchant marine. 1 am glad to see the hon. member's remarks were mostly of a questioning nature; he was looking for information, and was told that the matter came under the Department of Transport.
Representing the constituency of Queens-Lunenburg, where I am in t.he centre of marine activity, I have considerable local knowledge with regard to the movement and activity of our merchant seamen, whom I regard as perhaps the most important and vital of the men who are performing their duty on the Atlantic at the present time.
The hon. member concluded his remarks on the point in this way:
I believe someone should take hold of it, and do some organizing. To my mind it is silly to have men, after leaving their boats, drifting from one end of the country to the other, looking for other boats.
I thought yesterday the situation was not such as was portrayed by the hon. member, but I waited until this morning and took up the matter with Captain Arthur Randles who is in charge of this matter. He is a seagoing captain of great experience, one who served on the Cunard line, and a man who should know his job thoroughly. I discovered that this movement of merchant seamen was well organized. The men whom my hon. friend met on the train going to Nova Scotia had been members of a crew of a British ship which was being turned over to another nationality. The crew was brought to the eastern coast, to the manning pool. All our manning pools are within Canada, located in eastern Canadian ports.
Men are brought to the manning pools for several reasons. First, they can be properly
controlled and looked after. Second, their health can be checked and treatment given, if necessary. Third, they can be given basic pay while waiting for a ship. A ship may arrive in New York and may be two or three weeks in port if repairs are needed or if the return cargo is not ready or for many other reasons. It would be folly to keep the crew alongside that ship for that length of time. It is considered advisable not to allow a crew to scatter in a foreign port; it is thought better to keep them under control and supervision. Therefore they are brought to the manning pool at the rendezvous, the last port before the ships leave to cross the Atlantic. Many ships come there from United States ports with only part crews, and the complete crew is obtained at the port on the Atlantic coast. It is important that a ship which is to be a part of a convoy should not delay the convoy while getting a crew together. Crews must always be available at this special place, and that is why the merchant marine have established these manning pools on our coast.
The manning pools are operated at considerable expense and are vitally necessary in looking after seamen. I am told that the usual seaman's pay on ships is S100 a month, which is little enough. The pay for oil tankers is more because this work is quite dangerous. I do not want the idea to go abroad, and I do not think the hon. member intended that it should, that seamen were carried from one port to another, leaving no crew available for the ship on which they had arrived. Ships are arriving every day. A ship arriving to-day may expect to be in port three weeks. Its crew can be brought to the rendezvous port where they can be checked up and given a rest or put in hospital, if necessary. When the ship is ready to sail, another crew will be available.
I was glad to hear the minister say that in some cases the pay of our naval ratings and junior naval officers is to be increased. The junior officers felt that they deserved a little better treatment. During the last war a position in the navy was considered a rather comfortable berth. During the last war the Canadian navy was not to such a great extent engaged, and the men of the navy did not have to face the constant dangers faced by the soldiers overseas. But in this war, as the minister says, the navy is having the casualties and is facing the rigours of the north Atlantic in winter, the submarine menace and all the dangers of the sea. The men of the navy are facing great hazards, and they should be rewarded accordingly.
I would remind the committee that many seamen are being taken care of on the eastern

War Appropriation-Naval Services
coast. Over 500 shipwrecked seamen have been picked up and cared for within the last couple of months. Hon. members can see that it is a lively place as far as merchant seamen are concerned. So the merchant seamen and the navy deserve the best of treatment from the Canadian people.
Was the adjustment to which the minister referred in the case I mentioned due to a reclassification of the man's position, or will it apply to other storerooms across Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: As far as I understand, Mr. Pitman has not been reclassified. He is a naval stores officer. Reclassifications have been worked out in a great many cases, not merely at the dockyard at Halifax, but also at Esquimalt.

The minister gave us a break-down yesterday which included $52,-
720,000	for stores, equipment and supplies, and $34,166,000 for armament stores. Will the minister outline to the committee what machinery the department has to make sure that these supplies are up to standard? In connection with torpedoes and other things supplied to the naval department, is there a representative of the department in the armament factories to make inspections? What percentage of materials purchased during the past year were not up to standard?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I could not give my hon. friend specific instances, but I may say that we have inspection officers who go around inspecting the many things we buy. These officers insist that the articles be up to specification. If they are not, and cannot be brought up to the specifications by modification, they are immediately condemned. It would take me some little time to find out just how great this condemnation has been, but I can get the information for my hon. friend.

Are there inspectors in each armament firm producing materials for the navy, or are inspectors located only in some firms? What is the procedure in connection with the condemnation of materials? Is it sent back to ordnance?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I imagine it would not be accepted at all. I am not exactly sure whether we have a man in every little place, but the articles are inspected before we accept them.
Is there an inspection staff for all this material?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.
Is that part of the British purchasing commission?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Our organization is not nearly as large as that of the British purchasing commission which has a tremendous organization spread all over the country. However, in a general way the work is similar. All inspection branches are doing pretty much the same sort of work; they examine the material before it is finally accepted. If it is not according to specification, it is condemned unless it can be brought up to standard by some modification. That is what we do on a smaller scale, compared with the army or the British purchasing commission.
I have the assurance of the minister that all supplies are inspected by the naval authorities?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.

Before the present system of purchasing through the department of munitions was set up, and perhaps in the early stages of the war when the purchasing board was operating, I think under Mr. Vaughan, the navy did its own purchasing, as did national defence. Then this new system was established whereby the department requiring supplies and munitions and the like requisitioned the Department of Munitions and Supply. That department makes the contract, fixes the price and so forth, but the inspection is carried on by the department making the requisition. Is that not the procedure? Or is there a double inspection? I would not assume there was, but is there?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: In many cases there is a double inspection.

Suppose shells are required for the navy. They are ordered through the Department of Munitions and Supply on requisition from the navy. Does the navy have an inspection staff in the shell plant, or is the inspection done under the Department of Munitions and Supply? I know there is an inspection because I have seen it, but I just want to know the modus operandi.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
If you ask me about a given plant, I could not say at the moment whether we have inspectors there or not. Some plants do a very minor form of work, and we might not have an inspector there, but undoubtedly we would have supervision over the manufacture of shells. The branch of our department that is concerned with that work is under the particular charge of Captain Wood. Ships

War Appropriation-Naval Services
that were being built for us by the Department of Munitions and Supply would be inspected by the officers of another branch of the Department of Naval Services, who would watch their building, attend their trials, and finally pass upon them as having been properly built, and that inspection service would be in addition to whatever inspection the Department of Munitions and Supply might give.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The total number of discharges from the navy up to the end of last year was 1,537, and the number discharged as medically unfit, 933. We do provide work, where that is possible, for men who are partly unfit. I do not say that that is always possible, but I know we have one man at headquarters here who lost his leg in service, and he is still in the service, wearing an artificial limb. That is what we would try to do wherever possible.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.

Would the minister say
where they are being held, the subjects taught in those courses, the length of the courses, and whether those schools will be continued after the college is opened near Esquimalt next autumn?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Officers are trained to some extent at each one	of	the	vounteer reserve	divisions	inCanada, beginning at Charlottetown and going on to Saint John, Quebec, Montreal, and	so	on.	Some of the training of	the
officers would be undertaken there. The next stage in the officer's training if he is accepted, would be carried on at Halifax in the east or at Esquimalt in the west.

These courses will be carried on after the college at Esquimalt is opened, because that college	will	have a capacity	of only	onehundred cadets a year. The entry age is as low as sixteen. By itself that college would not	at	all	begin to fill the	needs of	the
Canadian navy, for officers.
The Minister of National Defence filed a syllabus of training for the officers under his department. Would the minister put on Hansard a copy of the syllabus which the naval officers take?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

Referring to the Spikenard, I believe that several of the pensonnel of the ship were saved. They were picked up and, I presume, taken to England. What happened after they arrived in England? In such cases are the men placed on other Canadian ships, or are they sent home to Canada?

speechtext: They probably received leave after they got ashore. Three or four of the men went to hospital, I think, and three or four did not need to go to hospital. They would come under the charge of the captain of the Niobe, Captain Agnew, and he would look after them.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is not a very easy question to answer. In the case of these particular men, if they were given leave to come home to Canada, I should think they would get passage on a Canadian corvette or destroyer. The practice of paying a man's leave from a foreign country to Canada is one that creates some difficulty, and there is no uniform rule about it in all three services. My hon. friend can see what problems it would lead to if we began to pay the transportation of men in large numbers from England to Canada. It would amount to a very great sum. On the other hand, we feel in the navy that if a ship has to put into a United States port-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I know, and if my hon. friend is speaking of that, that is another story. I thought he was asking whether transportation is paid to men who are given leave to come home to Canada.

We feel that if a ship puts into a United States port for a long refitting and has to be there for a month, it may be better to have the sailors return to their homes in Canada rather than to be kept in that port. Would the families of
those who lost their lives on the Spikenard be compensated? If so, what is the scale of compensation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
cannot give the scale of compensation, but it is the regular pension. The minister of pensions can give that. If a sailor is lost at sea his dependents receive exactly the same treatment as the dependents of a man killed on the battlefield, but what the scale may be in any given case I do not know. I have not the table here.

I have in mind a son who lost his life at the time the Spikenard was sunk. His family asked me if his mother would be allowed any compensation. Before he enlisted he had been one of the supporters of the family.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: In that case the pension is not a matter of right but is based upon certain principles, one of which is that he would have been the sole support of his parents if he had been saved and had returned home. Suppose at some future time the mother should become dependent on the public for support. What I want to know is, between now and that time, while not receiving anything, what would be her status? Would she be entitled later on?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: If he had contributed to her support before serving in the forces and she was not able to earn her own livelihood, she would be considered eligible.

There

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes.

speechtext: We have argued a great deal about that, but we were beaten down finally. We have to provide the equipment, and pay for it, so that it is ours.

speechtext: Yes. We began in a small way, doing work for them, and ended by paying for the whole thing.

And the service of the crew for the guns?

speechtext:
In

speechtext:
I

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I

this reason. In the air force it stops immediately. I have in mind a young man who enlisted in the R.C.A.F. and on reaching England was apparently transferred to the R.A.F. He was there only a short time and was sent to Gibraltar or Malta.

speechtext: That is the R.A.F.?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

speechtext: That is in the R.A.F. That does not come under the Canadian regulations. We have our own regulations which are different from those.

This is probably not the
right time to ask how he got out of the R.C.A.F. into the R.A.F. I should like to know whether on going into the R.A.F. he lost all rights that belonged to him under the R.C.AJF.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There are many Canadians in the R.A.F. Some are on Canadian rates of pay-most of them, I believe. I thought my hon. friend was referring to a Canadian who had joined the R.A.F., becoming an out-and-out member of it.

There is an anomaly in the pension law which I can best illustrate by taking the case of a member of the naval service. Our pension legislation now in existence came into effect a year ago in pursuance of a report of a special committee under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macmillan). The effect of the legislation on members of the armed forces was to change the pension law as it stood in 1940 when under the terms of an order in council there was in effect the principle that obtained in the original Pension Act of 1919. The feature of which I wish to speak is the so-called insurance principle, sometimes called the "incurred during service" principle. Under that principle, once a man enlisted the country became responsible for him. There was one exception, misconduct, but subject to misconduct the country in effect took the responsibility of insuring the man so that if any injury occurred to him during service he, or in case of death his dependents, became entitled to pension. But instead of that principle there was adopted what is commonly called the "attributable to service" principle, which meant that the injured man, in the event of disability, or his dependents in the event of his death, had to show that his injury or death arose out of or was directly connected with his military service.
Taking the case of men serving in the Canadian navy, if these men are injured or
2266	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Naval Services
killed outside the territorial waters of Canada they or their dependents are entitled to compensation. It does not affect the case whether their injury or death was due to accident or to something that occurred in the course of hostilities. If a man in the Canadian naval service is killed while in Canada his dependents will not necessarily obtain compensation, nor in case of injury will he necessarily be entitled to compensation.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Unless it was a result of service.

Unless that injury or death arose out of or was connected with his naval service. In other words if a man takes influenza or has appendicitis, unless he can show, which in many cases is impossible, that his influenza or appendicitis was occasioned by his service in the navy, he or his dependents are not entitled to compensation. If he is accidentally killed while out motoring, likewise, unless he was on some work connected with his service, there is no provision for compensation. Of course the same principle is also in effect in the army and the air force.
I suggest that whatever may have been the reasons for this anomaly in our pension law in the past, to-day, under the changed conditions, they no longer apply. The war has spread to the Pacific as well as the Atlantic; enemy submarines operate in our coastal and territorial waters. There seems to be no reason why men in the naval service in Canada should be under a disability or be discriminated against in comparison with members of our naval service serving in England or in the West Indies. The same is true of members of the Canadian air force and members of the Canadian army who, while ready to go overseas, die in consequence of some injury contracted during their service but not directly attributable to their service. All these men should have the same protection that was accorded to men who served in the last war. It is almost impossible for a medical man or for anybody to prove to a medical tribunal that a man's death, occurring say in consequence of appendicitis, was attributable to service. Although his service, however, may not have been the immediate cause, the fatality may have been due to the changed conditions under which he had to live when he became a member of the armed forces. In other words some months after a man joins the army or the navy in perfectly good health, he suffers an attack of illness from some internal condition which, while it cannot be shown to have been directly attributable to service, nevertheless may have been occasioned 
or brought on by changed diet, changed lodging or changed living conditions.
I know it may be said that there is provision for a compassionate allowance in certain cases, but I submit that is not good enough. Members of the active service force who are injured during service should be entitled to pension if disability occurs during service, not on compassionate grounds, not as a matter of charity or hand-out, but as a reward for valuable service rendered to the country. These men or their dependents should not have to prove necessity in order to qualify for compensation, because if they do, in many cases those who are most deserving would not obtain compensation. Their circumstances might be necessitous, but their pride would preclude them from applying on those grounds.
We were all pleased at the minister's announcement to-day that new naval regulations will bring to parity as far as possible the pay of those in the naval service and that of those in other branches of the armed forces. I suggest to the minister that some attempt be made to take up now the question of the compensation to which members of the naval service, as well as those of the other armed services, should become entitled in the event of disability.
Would the minister care to tell the committee if corvettes are used in convoy work or for protection against submarines?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

speechtext: The broadcast to which my hon. friend refers was made by Engineer Captain Stephens, I think.

speechtext: I did not see the text of the broadcast before it was delivered, and I would not care to attempt to answer the question definitely, as to whether the engineering department consulted the Department of National War Services before making the appeal. Proof of that is to be found in the fact that it has been necessary to send certain refitting and repair work to other places to be done. What are the hours of employment at the Halifax dockyard, for instance? Certainly work in these three categories is required to be done in our dockyards. I should like the minister to tel! us the number employed at the Halifax dockyard in that work, and how many shifts are working each day.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot tell my hon. friend that we do as well as the Portsmouth dockyard, where he found twenty thousand men working three shifts a day. I do not think we can approach
that record. I should like to get specific information on that point, and bring it down on Monday.

As a

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think that statement was made the other day with reference to the Halifax shipyard, which is another matter altogether. I am speaking of the naval dockyard. There are not three full shifts a day. On the other hand I would not want to say that there is not one full shift and other partial shifts. I believe one of the problems there is a shortage of skilled foremen, and that sort of thing; but there are not three full shifts. On the other hand, I think it is a little better than one eight-hour shift; but I should like to get the exact information.
Are all repairs required to Canadian ships made in Canada, or do some ships have to be sent outside to be repaired?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Some are repaired outside of Canada-in Newfoundland, in Great Britain, and some even in United States ports.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I did not want to give exact figures with regard to any particular ships. speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: What was the vessel, a merchant ship?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am not sure that it was a warship.

No, I
would not suppose it was, from the name. speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall be glad to do that. Offhand I have not heard of the case of the Claire Lilley, but I shall find out about it. It might not be in my department at all, but I shall get the fullest possible information.

A few days ago an hon. member asked what right nontMr. R, B. Hanson.]
British countries had to order their nationals domiciled in Canada to undertake compulsory service in their own armed forces. I have had occasion to look up the law on this subject, and to hon. members to whom it might be of interest I would refer them to Hansard of May 1, 1941, where the Prime Minister gave a conclusive answer to the same question when asked by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. From that answer it appears that such countries can bring the call for compulsory service to the attention of the nationals, but they cannot exercise any compulsion within Canada in order to induce them to respond to the call. The Prime Minister continued:
The national of the foreign government can refuse to respond to the call, without incurring any penalties within this country. On the other hand he will not be able to embark on a ship flying the flag of his home country or enter its territories ^without subjecting himself to prosecution in his own country.
That is the situation.

I have had the privilege of visiting Halifax harbour and barracks on only one occasion but, since my home is in the vicinity of Esquimalt, I have been there on many occasions. I have noticed at both points that while there is a large number of civilians working, there is very poor restaurant accommodation. Our men have been asking for better accommodation, and I should like to know if the situation has been remedied.
Another matter which seemed apparent was the congestion within the barracks itself. A number of bunkhouses appeared to be built very close to each other. Is there any real necessity for having these bunkhouses, accommodating a large number of men, built side by side. I believe one of the bunkhouses at Halifax harbour has been destroyed since the time of my visit.
Is there any necessity for having hospitals built within that area? It seems to me we are running an unnecessary risk which could be avoided by spreading out a little more. Additional buildings are being erected at Esquimalt, and in my opinion they are being built too close to the other buildings, having regard to protection of our men.
I believe, too, we have not yet any balloon barrages, or any type of protection which should be above these barracks to protect the men as much as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I shall look into these matters. I do not believe it is desirable to have the hospitals out of the general area in which the troops are located. It must be remembered that the problem of discipline and the control of men

War Appropriation-Naval Services
is always important. While I agree that the buildings should not be crowded closely together, still I think they should all be within the same general area, for the sake of the better discipline which can be effected in that way.
I shall look into the question of restaurant accommodation for civilians at Esquimalt. The balloon barrage does not come within my department. On the assumption that balloon barrage protection is desirable or necessary in some of the coastal cities, a subject concerning which there is considerable doubt, it would not be the duty of the navy, but rather be that of one of the other forces to provide such barrage.
I understand considerable ship repairing is being done at the port of Louisburg. Is any repairing being done to naval ships at that port?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not think any extensive repairs are being done to naval ships. There might be some small or running repairs which could be made there; but there is, as far as I know, no dry dock or marine railway at Louisburg. Consequently only light repairs could be made. However, some merchant ships are putting in there, and it may well be that some naval ships, too, have had minor repairs done. I should hope that that would be the case.

The minister has told us
about the elaborate programme for the con-itruction of naval vessels during the coming year, and about the number of vessels constructed during the past year. All hon. members realize the great need for these vessels, and that they should be built as quickly as possible. I believe the public has been quite concerned in the past year over the great number of labour disputes in Canada. Have these labour disputes in any way materially affected the navy's building programme? I realize, of course, that such disputes come under the Department of Labour, but they also affect our war effort. While we realize that the men should and must receive the proper wages for their labour, we have been quite concerned over sympathetic strikes where large numbers of men go out on strike perhaps because some one man has been dismissed by reason of lack of knowledge of the work he is supposed to perform. How many work hours have been lost on naval construction in the past year on account of such strikes in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I shall try to get that information from the Minister of Munitions and Supply. I wish he were here. I know he intends to be here
because he expects to reach some of his expenditures. The hon. member will, however, understand that when we want a ship we specify the kind of ship and have the plans drawn up. Then the Department of Munitions and Supply arranges for the building of it. Consequently the matter of days lost through labour disputes would be one within the knowledge of that department rather than of mine. Of course anything that keeps men away from work for two or three days interferes to that extent with the swift and complete building of the ship.

I should like to bring up something which perhaps is within the jurisdiction of the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe). I think the ministry should give some indication of what the position is with regard to labour ;n the city of Halifax, particularly in respect of the shipyards and the longshoremen. I believe a rather disturbing situation has arisen there. While a discussion of this matter may not be germane to the minister's estimates, it may be of some interest to this country to know that as recently as April 30, 1942, order in council P.C. 3511 was passed on the recommendation of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), invoking the provisions of both the War Measures Act and the National Resources Mobilization Act. Under this order in council the longshoremen in the port of Halifax are being regimented, or should I say "conscripted", for the first time. The principle of compulsion has been inaugurated, and the order provides for the imposition of fines and penalties for breaches of the order made by the controller.
I do not know the reason for the enactment of this order in council but I do know that it is the most advanced piece of legislation with respect to labour ever passed by this government by means of order in council with parliament in session and without any reference to parliament. I want hon. members to read this order in council over the weekend and to endeavour to understand its implications. I would refer them to the preamble and to the subject matter as covered by section 3.

Is it in the Canada
Gazettet

I do not know; I never see the Canada Gazette. I get copies of the orders in council passed under the War Measures Act and I read as many of them as possible. When this one reached my desk yesterday I thought it contained most drastic provisions, and I thought some explanation was due to the house

War Appropriation-Naval Services
and the country with respect to the underlying policy. I do not say that the position is not justified, for I do not know what the circumstances are. But I do know that the proposals contained in this order in council are the most drastic with relation to labour that have been enacted since the war began or even before. I direct the attention of hon. gentlemen to section 3 which covers the powers of the controller and to section 12 which covers the modus operandi and the allocation of labour to individuals working in the harbour. This section has eight subsections. Section 13 grants protection to the controller and any person acting for or under his authority and declares, under the authority of the War Measures Act and the Mobilization Act, that the controller or any such person "shall not be liable to any person for anything done or omitted in the exercise or purported exercise of any power or authority from time to time vested in the controller." He is made a czar.
That is in most orders now.
It is a drastic provision.
Oh, yes.

Section 14 of the order provides:
All persons, companies, organizations, associations or agencies

I think that covers the whole gamut of human relations.
-directly or indirectly engaged or concerned in shiploading' operations in the port-
Meaning the port of Halifax.
-shall in all matters act upon-
That is the compulsion.
-and in accordance with the directions, orders and decisions given or made by the controller under this order.
The first question that naturally arises is: what was the occasion for the enactment of such drastic legislation? I do not say that the occasion did not warrant the action, because I do not know, but I think it is due to the public that the true position should be made known. We should be told why this order was enacted when the house was in session. Was it necessary to act so quickly that parliament could not be consulted? This is a direct regimentation of labour, mandatory in character, with breaches punishable on summary conviction by fine or imprisonment or both. The provisions with respect to punishment will be found in section 16, which reads:
Any person, company, organization, association or agency as aforesaid who, or which, contravenes or fails to comply with any pro-

vision of this order or with any direction, order or decision given or made by the controller under this order shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding $500 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three months or to both such fine and such imprisonment.
That may be necessary. I do not know, but I do invite the ministry to tell us why such drastic legislation was enacted by order in council while this house was in session and why the governor in council took upon itself the power to impose fine and imprisonment for a breach of a civil order. Is that to be the policy of the government for the future with regard to labour? I hold no especial brief for labour, but I want to see fair play. Is any other class in the country being dealt with in the same way? Yes, there is. There are other civil provisions in respect of breaches of orders in council which were passed by this government while parliament was in session. There are many of them, but this is the first time that this principle has been applied to organized labour, and the ministry must justify itself. Has organized labour failed in the national emergency? Is it necessary in the public interest that this order should be passed? Let us know the circumstances so that the house and the country may judge. I am not passing judgment on the policy; I am simply questioning the reason for it.
It is our right and duty to call attention to these matters. We should not allow this sort of thing to pass unnoticed. I am not approaching it in a spirit of censure, and I am certainly not approaching it in a spirit of praise. I want to know what the facts are, and I want to approach whatever consideration I give to them with as judicial a mind as I can summon to my support. I invite the minister to tell us the reason why this was done. The Minister of Labour is not at the moment in his seat. He is the sponsor of this thing, but I have no doubt that the demand, if there was such a demand, came from other departments.
So far as I know, organized labour in this country have made their contribution to the war. So far as I understand their position, they are not satisfied with certain things which have been done; they are not satisfied with government policy.
May I pause here for a moment to pay tribute to the work of a man who in the course of a lifetime's performance of duty was suddenly stricken yesterday with illness. I refer to Mr. Tom Moore. I have known him for many years. I am glad to say that I have always found his views with respect to the relations between capital and labour, and the relations of labour with the government, sane

War Appropriation-Naval Services
and sound. I regret more than I can say that at this difficult time, in the performance of his duty, in endeavouring to explain matters to those whom he represents, he should have temporarily at least fallen by the wayside. I certainly hope-and in expressing this hope I am sure that it will be the wish of everybody within sound of my voice-that his disability is only temporary.
Labour for the most part, I think, has satisfactorily performed its functions in this difficult war period through which we are passing. There are perhaps exceptions. I have no doubt that there is a left wing in labour, as there is in most bodies, and I certainly have never welcomed certain agents who have come into this country. But that is just in passing.
I think the government owe to this house and certainly to the country an explanation why legislation of this kind is passed by order in council while parliament is in session, legislation confined, if you will, to a narrow basis, to the port of Halifax, and I invite the minister to give us an explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
regret that I am not able to comply with the hon. gentleman's request. Matters dealing with longshoremen and labour conditions are matters for the Minister of Labour. I think we should leave them to him to deal with. I believe he could explain the genesis of the order in council, certainly much better than I could. We do not employ longshoremen. If there are naval craft to be attended to, we attend to them ourselves. I do not know whether my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply has anything to say about the matter. I think the explanation of the order in council had better be left to the Minister of Labour.

Mr. Chairman, in rising
to say a word on this matter I should like first to associate myself with the remarks of the leader of the opposition in regard to the sudden illness of Mr. Tom Moore, President of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada. I have known Mr. Moore for many years and have been associated with him at times in his work, and I join most heartily in the hope expressed by the leader of the opposition that Mr. Moore's illness may be only temporary.
I am glad that the leader of the opposition has raised the question he did because in my own feeble way I have been trying ever since the beginning of the war to impress upon this house and the country that one of the chief obstacles to our war effort has
been the refusal of the government to take labour into its confidence and to make it a partner.
When in February last the executive of the trades and labour congress of Canada met certain members of the cabinet to put before them the legislative programme of the congress for this year, the Prime Minister frankly admitted that the government had not cooperated with labour as much as it should have done. But despite that, the government has not changed its policy.
The leader of the opposition has referred to the order in council. I must admit that I have never seen it, and I do not know how the leader of the opposition got it, unless it was sent to him as a special favour or unless he made application to the clerk of the privy council for it.

I think all orders in council under the War Measures Act are sent as a matter of courtesy to the leader of the opposition from the registrar of the legislative committee of the cabinet. I am sure I cannot read them all.

I hope we shall all get a copy of the order in council at an early date. But let me tell the leader of the opposition and the members of this house that this is not the first order in council of this kind which has been passed since the war began. My hon. friend the member for Royal, I think it was, asked a question in regard to the amount of time lost through strikes. If one considers the non-cooperative policy of the government and the anti-labour policy of Canadian employers, it is amazing how few strikes we have had and how little time has been lost in that way in Canada since the war began. Whenever a little time is lost through a strike we all know about it at once through headlines in the press, but we do not hear of the time that is continually being lost-far more time than is lost by strikes-through lack of proper organization in industrial plants and matters of that kind over which the workers have no control.
Last September, while a number of disputes in shipyards were being heard by conciliation boards appointed by the Department of Labour, that department appointed a royal commission to investigate the shipyards in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. As I have pointed out before, the members of that royal commission, three lawyers, Mr. MacDonald, of Dalhousie university, Senator Gouin, of Ottawa or Montreal, and Mr. Barlow of Ontario, were appointed without any prior consultation whatsoever with

War Appropriation-Naval Services
organized labour. Some time after it was appointed to deal with one or two shipyards, its powers were extended to cover all the shipyards in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. On November 24 the commission reported to the Minister of Labour recommending an increased wage scale for all the shipyards concerned. This matter was under discussion for some time; then suddenly on January 26 the government, by order in council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Labour, ignored altogether the report of its royal commission and the scale of wages it had recommended, and for the first time in Canada's history, so far as I know, set a wage scale by order in council. Not only did they set the wage scale for certain workers by order in council, but in the same order they gave the Minister of Labour the right to set wages for any category of labour not already mentioned in the schedule attached to the order in council, at whatever rate he might consider fair and reasonable. As I pointed out some time ago, that is doing just the very opposite to what the government at the beginning of the war did by order in council. By order in council P.C. 2685 the government gave its blessing to the principle of collective bargaining; but here, by order in council, it has completely destroyed collective bargaining, because there can be no collective bargaining under an order in council.
If there is anything that is amazing in our whole war effort it is the fact that labour has acted as reasonably as it has done considering the treatment it has received; and undoubtedly the reason that labour has acted as reasonably as it has, is that labour realizes that it has a stake in the winning of this war. There must be some one in the Department of Labour of late, who, whenever a case comes up involving some problem that requires consideration and cooperation with labour, immediately says, "We had better settle it by order in council". There must be someone in the department with considerable influence who takes that attitude. I do not know who the party is but in some way or other that person must be rooted out, or the Minister of Labour will have to take the responsibility for what has been done and is being done in his name. I have not seen the order in council to which the leader of the opposition has referred. I will make it my business to see it as early as I can, and I shall have something further to say about it. This order, I understand, refers to longshore work. I wonder if the Department of Labour has heard what has

happened in the old country with regard to longshoremen. Longshoremen to-day are in the service of the government with a stated wage, whether they work or not. That is something that Ernest Bevin won in a dispute in 1921. For a long time it was not given effect to; he had to wait twenty years until he came into office himself before the organization he represented received what they were given by a board set up by the government.
I have mentioned the failure of the government to cooperate with labour. I have in my hand a report by the executive of the trades and labour congress of Canada, of which Mr. Moore is president, on order in council P.C. 8253, the wage-fixing order. In this report the executive states:
This conference further expresses its regret that any representative of the government should create such a misleading impression in the public mind, that labour had in any manner been a party to the formulation of the policies incorporated in order in council P.C. 8253.
That was in connection with a statement made in a radio address by the former minister of labour that this order had been discussed with organized labour before it was passed. The report goes on:
At the outset this conference reiterates and wishes to make definite and clear that organized labour throughout the whole of Canada as represented by the trades and labour congress of Canada has pledged its fullest support to the government of Canada in all steps essential to prosecute the war to a successful conclusion to the end that freedom, right and justice shall prevail over the nazi forces of aggression. . . . This declared policy was made in good faith and has been faithfully observed.
It must be pointed out, however, that the unwillingness of the federal government to accept the proffered cooperation of the representatives of organized workers makes it increasingly difficult for them to give effect to that policy.
This is the considered opinion not of a left-wing of the Canadian labour movement, but of conservative responsible officials of the largest labour organization in Canada. Not only that, but they said in connection with the national labour supply council, which has recently been abolished:
The conference considered that the national labour supply council was not functioning as had been expected,-
But listen to this.
-but that in many instances it had been used to mislead the public as to the attitude of organized labour respecting the government's labour policies, and in that way the members acting thereon had been placed in a false position. This opinion was expressed in the following resolution which was unanimously adopted:

War Appropriation-Naval Services
Whereas the national labour supply council was created by order in council P.C. 2686 of June, 1940, by the present government for the purpose of acting in an advisory capacity regarding matters affecting labour and industry during the war emergency;
And whereas many questions of national importance have been referred to this council for advice, and in many instances, other matters of equal or greater importance have been dealt with in other quarters and the national labour supply council ignored;
Whereas, generally the advice and recommendations of the council have not been accepted by the government or its ministers, which indicates that its services are evidently of no value as further demonstrated by the manner in which order in council P.C. 8253 was enacted.
Therefore be it resolved, that the representatives of the affiliated organizations of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada herewith request that the order in council under which the national labour supply council was established be revoked.
Could there be a greater condemnation of the government's policy toward organized labour than that resolution? Possibly this is not the time to deal fully with this matter, but that time will come, and I assure this committee that the question of the government's labour policy will be dealt with.
