speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have not much to add except that on the east coast General Elkins is in command of the whole area. My hon. friend's question was, I think, particularly directed to whether General Elkins could order ships of the Canadian navy out to sea. In a strict sense he could not do that; I am so informed by the chief of naval staff. I do not know that any army commander would endeavour to designate particular ships, because he is not familiar with the operation of ships. What I fancy might be done would be that the general would say, "I want a combined force of ships, planes and land forces for a certain purpose", and he would ask the naval commander, "what in your judgment would be the correct number of ships and that sort of thing?" That, I imagine, is what General Elkins would do. Strictly speaking, he is in what is called strategic control of the whole coast, but he does not exercise or attempt to exercise powers over the actual disposition of individual ships. That is a matter which is still under the control of the chief of naval staff and the admiral commanding on the Atlantic coast.

Mr. Chairman, the leader of the opposition brought up the matter of this order in council, and I think this committee has a right to an explanation from the Minister of Labour in regard to it, because I believe it is just one more step tending to lessen the importance of this parliament in the eyes of the people of Canada. To me this is one of the most unusual of the departures from the ordinary rules of law that have characterized the activities of this government, and I add my protest in support of the stand taken by the leader of the opposition. I protest against the tendency of this government to act with cavalier disregard of and contempt for the rights of parliament. This order in council goes further than any other passed so far. Up to the present time acts of parliament have been suspended, amended in part or in whole, and even abrogated by order in council, and I may add that we on this side of the house have been endeavouring to secure information in regard to the statutes thus affected, but as yet we have been unable to get it, though [Mr. Macdonald (Kingston City).J
the Prime Minister has stated that certain acts of parliament have been effected as indicated.
Under this legislation labour is placed in a position which cannot be justified. I am not one of those who believe in raising class against class, in pointing out the great contribution of labour and at the same time ridiculing the contribution made by the industrialists of this country. Both have contributed to the effort; they have worked in partnership, and I condemn those who would endeavour, in time of war, to secure support for themselves, by pleading for one class as against another or by endeavouring to cast aspersions upon the great industrialists, of whom some are known as dollar-a-year men, who are serving this country fairly and honestly. Labour has done fine work. So have the industrialists. But I do think this piece of legislation is not fair to labour. It reveals a tendency to disregard the rights of individuals engaged in labour which, if not protested against, may well lead to a state of regimentation one does not care to contemplate.
This is the first mobilization by compulsion and by locality. It is limited territorially. The rule of law under which we operate gives every person equality under the law, but this legislation by order in council makes it an offence to do certain things in Halifax, places labour under compulsion in Halifax, while a different law prevails in all the other seaports of Canada. I protest against the principle of an order in council such as this, which is retroactive in part and applicable to only one section of Canada. If it is to be of assistance to the war effort, then make it applicable to all seaports. To make such provisions applicable to only one place; to give any individual the power to control and dictate to labour as to how it shall act, what it shall do, and so on, is a departure from British constitutional principles and a denial of the liberty of the subject. Section 3 of this order in council provides that the controller shall have power and authority-
[DOT]-to give directions to, and to make orders, and decisions binding upon, all persons, companies, organizations, associations and agencies engaged or concerned in shiploading or unloading at the port of Halifax with respect to all matters, whether general or special, other than wage rates, affecting working and hiring conditions, practices and methods in connection with shiploading and unloading operations.
Then it goes on and destroys the entire right of the individual to hire as he will. Under the provisions of this order in council men are going to be hired not as individuals but, if I may use the expression, in bulk, for section 12 provides:

War Appropriation-Naval Services
The present system of daily hiring of individuals working at the site of the work is hereby abolished and there shall be substituted therefor a new system of hiring which, subject to such alterations as the controller may deem expedient, shall embody the following principles. . . .
What controller?

A controller set up by the governor in council to control the longshoremen in the city of Halifax. Then it goes on to provide that there shall be set up a central dispatching agency:
The present active working personnel of the port shall be divided into fixed gangs with named gang bosses; longshoremen shall hereafter be hired in gangs and exclusively through the dispatching agency.
Just picture the situation. Only those are to be hired who come exclusively through a dispatching agency set up by the government. This government, which is so fearful of compulsion in so many matters, by order in council has done something which constitutes an invasion of the rights of the individual that in fny opinion cannot be justified. When we speak about labour and production-and no doubt we will be hearing more about this -is labour responsible to-day for the decrease in production that has occurred in some parts of Canada? Or is it the lack of governmental organization; is it the bottlenecks which have been created because of the fact that materials are not being received? Members of this house are receiving letters from persons employed in various factories in Canada in which we have been told that men in some war plants have little or no work to do because of the shortage of materials.

Only in government
operated plants.

I am not speaking about government operated plants. I am speaking now of plants engaged in the manufacture of war materials, and I have particularly in mind plants engaged in the manufacture of aeroplanes. We cannot get any direct answer from the government; we are simply told that it cannot be so. I do not believe that statements coming from men working in factories in various parts of Canada that there is no work, or they are working only part time, because of the shortage of materials, would be made unless there is some foundation therefor. I suggest this, that instead of bringing into effect while parliament is in session an order in council which controls the individual and interferes with his rights to such an extent as to render him powerless-instead of introducing legislation like that while parliament is in
session, by the backdoor route of an order in council, this government should ask for and would get the cooperation of labour. Canada should be assured that the men engaged in industiy and those working in war factories should have the opportunity of contributing to the very limit, by operating a twenty or twenty-four hour day.
The Minister of National Defence for Naval Services to-day said that he needed ships. But he said our factories are not operating full time. I ask the minister what is being done in order to increase the production of ships in Canada. Does the naval department believe there should be wooden ships produced as mine-sweepers, and the like?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They are being produced.
In Canada? When the minister replies would he say when that production started, to what extent it is being encouraged by the government, and to what extent wooden vessels are being used?

My hon. friend has, if he will forgive me, stepped pretty heavily into my own field of production. I think I should say a few words at this time. I am astonished that a gentleman who only to-day has been demanding conscription, and immediate conscription, objects so seriously to an arrangement which has a certain degree of compulsion as applied to longshoremen at Halifax. In war time the rights of the individual must on occasions be subordinated to the rights of the state.
Does the minister say that is conscription of the men in Halifax? Is that what it is?

No. But I say my hon. friend was demanding conscription, and he objects to the orderly feature of compulsion. The position at Halifax is this-and if the Minister of Labour were here he would be the proper man to answer it. A situation arose there that was just as bad for the men themselves as it was for the other interests concerned. The arrangements that were made there were made by mutual consent. In Halifax a tremendous number of boats have to load and unload. The delay of a boat alongside a dock may be just as serious as the loss of one boat. At least the delay of boats for three or four days is as serious as the loss of one boat by submarine sinking.
A situation arose under which too much time was lost in Halifax. I think it was a year ago that by agreement with labour Mr. COMMONS
War Appropriation-Naval Services
Vincent Macdonald was placed in the position of being the arbitrator 'of all matters of stevedoring. Since that time there has been some improvement, but in recent months we have had crews turn up without key men -certain winchmen and certain labourers who must be with the crew, otherwise the crew cannot function. We have had cases where a crew would turn up, but because of that winchman they would have to be sent home; they could not function. We have had cases where winchmen would turn up, but an insufficient number of labourers would turn up for the crew to function. It was a disorganized state of affairs. Some arrangement had to be made so that we could be sure that when a shift came on it would come on complete, with the proper organization to go to work.
The Minister of Labour went to Halifax and spent some time there consulting longshoremen organizations. He met the longshoremen in mass public meetings, and the result was this order in council. The order in council is an improvement for the men. It insured to the men that when they reported for work in Halifax they would be able to work, and it insured to the ships lying alongside-
After reporting for work, if for some reason work was stopped a few hours and the men had nothing to do, they would receive their pay anyway, would they not?

Yes, under this arrangement. A number of concessions were made. The men have always wanted a hiring hall in Halifax. The fact that there were several stevedoring organizations operating there led to the continued lack of a hiring hall. The hiring hall of course helps in the organization and the dispatch of crews.

The same as on the
railway.

It is not the same as on the railway, but it is the same system as has been working with great satisfaction in Vancouver for a number of years. The arrangements I am sure are much more satisfactory in labour to-day than they were before this order in council was passed.
Hitler stated the same thing about what he was doing.

Nevertheless my hon. friends opposite think nothing of conscripting men for the army. Men on the job, when they are under charter, are on pay and under discipline. I know no reason in war time why it is
IMr. Howe.]
criminal to put key men in industiy under discipline, especially if it is done by mutual consent, as this was.

Does the
minister say this was agreed to by the longshoremen?
Yes, certainly.

Does he now state that the policy of the government is to conscript free men for industry in this
way?

No; I am talking about a particular situation arranged by mutual consent, and an arrangement concerning which many statements have been made in this house which are wholly uncalled for. It is a policy which is not applied generally; it is applied in a particular place.
It is just a beginning, like other steps you take. It is one feeble step at the beginning.

Does my hon. friend object? He is quite convinced, I am sure, that it is quite fair to take certain men and say to them, "You go in the army." Does he say it is unfair to take other men and say, "You must work in industry"?
No, I did not say that. But here is a specific case, in a particular area, where men are told they must either go to work or go to gaol.

A man does not need to qualify as a longshoreman unless he wishes to. If he wishes to leave the profession he is free to do it. But as long as he holds a card as a longshoreman, and is paid a longshoreman's rates, and receives recognition by longshoremen, he must accept in every particular the discipline that goes with the work of a longshoreman. If that is conscription, then make the most of it. When a man signs on to work he is subject to the discipline of the job. When he signs on as a longshoreman at Halifax he is subject to the discipline of the longshoreman. There is no law enforcing him, as I see it. He does not have to sign up; if he wishes to quit, he can quit.
"Accept it or starve."

Starve 1 starve I-my hon.
friend should apologize for that. Who starves in this country because he does not work on a particular job?
I will say this, because that is a challenge-

Quite.

War Appropriation-Naval Services

I did not wish to engender any heat. But the effect of the policy of this government with respect to a certain class of young men in this country is "get into the army or starve". I have said that in this house more than once, and it is well known to the membership. I put myself in the judgment of the members of this house if that is not a correct statement of the position as a result of the policy of this government with respect to certain of our citizenship. I approached the matter through the front door but the government approached it by the indirect route. The effect of the government's policy is that certain young men must go in the army or starve.
My hon. friend makes the dogmatic statement that certain men must go into the army or starve. There may be one man who has starved.
That is beside the point.
You are talking nonsense and you know it.
I ask the minister to withdraw that. Am I in the habit of talking nonsense? I place myself in the judgment of the minister. I appeal to him.
Very infrequently.

I try to keep my feet on the ground. I try to be fair to the government. I have tried to help this government on many occasions. I tried to help the Minister of National Defence .the other night and I am sure he was grateful. I am not sure what is going to happen to me as a result.
Try to help me.

Yes, on the proper occasion, of course I will. The minister knows he does not have to appeal to me to do that. My one instinct is to do anything and everything I can to help the war effort. But I tell the minister frankly; I tell this house and I tell the people of Canada that I was shocked when I read the order in council passed in the secrecy of the council chamber and stumbled upon by me. As far as I know, no publicity was given to it in the press of this country.
It has not been printed.
We could not get a printed copy.

It has
been mimeographed. You can get a copy.
We have a copy now.

There may be absolute justification for it. I thought I approached the consideration of this matter with judicial fairness. That was the approach I intended to make. Does the minister say that there exists in the port of Halifax a situation which demanded that this be done?
Yes.
All right. That is the first question. Was it necessary to put into effect the underlying principle of this order in council because of the attitude of the longshoremen at Halifax?
The longshoremen agreed to it.

If they agreed to it, why was not the policy of having a round-table conference carried out? Why was not a working arrangement with the men arrived at instead of enunciating the principle contained in this order and making it a criminal act for the men who do not obey it? W7hy should they be made to submit themselves to the courts of this country as quasi criminals? I simply cannot accept that. It is contrary to my sense of reasoning. It is contrary to common sense. It does not add up. That is why I brought the matter before parliament.
It is no different from what they do in Great Britain.
That does not excuse us. Have they done it in the United States?
They are not so far into the war in the United States. .

I cannot reconcile the view that the longshoremen of Halifax accepted this order and knew what they were agreeing to, as the minister suggests. I am not questioning his word, because he should know and I do not. I put my statement in the form of an interrogatory. Did the longshoremen of Halifax know what was going to be in this order in council? I cannot for a moment think they did. Were the terms of the order in council submitted to the longshoremen or to their legal adviser? I assume they had one. Did they properly understand what they were agreeing to?

I addressed the owners,
and I discussed with the executive board of the union the original, basic order in council. I addressed the longshoremen and we enjoyed ourselves. I have been associated with them all my life; that is, with the rank and

the officials. We discussed the order in council for three hours in a building in the city of Halifax.
That does not answer my question. Was the concrete order in council submitted to the counsel for the longshoremen, and did he and they understand it?
The terms of it were discussed and agreed upon.
What does the minister of Mines and Resources know about this?
What do you know?

I am
trying to get information. I shall know a lot more about it long before my friend over there does. That interjection was quite uncalled for.

May I say with great
respect to the leader of the opposition that he asked a question. All I know, of course, is the information that was passed along.
You have some hearsay information; that is all.

Not hearsay. I think I
can make this comment, that I can claim to know as much about it as the leader of the opposition appears to do.

The minister knows what his colleague reported. That is what I would anticipate, and in law that is hearsay evidence. I do not suppose I can make the minister understand what hearsay is technically, but that is what it is to a lawyer. The minister is a layman, and we are dealing with a technical question when we are dealing with the law of evidence. I put it again to the Minister of Labour:	Did the
longshoremen of Halifax understand the concrete terms of this order in council, and did they understand that for a violation of one of its terms they were submitting themselves to a fine or imprisonment or both?

It is a fundamental
principle of British law that you cannot have one law for the rich and one law for the poor dealing with-
What has that to do with it?

Let me finish-dealing with the same subject. This applies both to the shipowners and to the longshoremen. I think it may be stated fairly that in the main the difficulties have been with the shipowners, with the stevedoring companies. You cannot

impose a fine on one side and not on the other. This matter was discussed frankly and freely with both sides.
The basis of the order in council?
The original order in council that laid down the basic principles of this order in council.
Was this one discussed?
There was no objection from the longshoremen.
Did they know about it?

Let the longshoremen speak for themselves. It is fundamental that ships have to be turned round. I went there and saw how they were hiring longshoremen, picking them out like sheep. They were using the system they used fifty years ago. What we have tried to do is to institute a system similar to the one on the Pacific coast. They have hiring halls there, but instead of the hiring halls at Halifax being under the jurisdiction of the employers, they will be under the jurisdiction of the Department of Labour. This is similar to what Mr. Churchill did in connection with a similar situation in Great Britain. As he stated, the safety of the state is paramount. These ships have to be turned round, and it was necessary to reorganize the port of Halifax so that the ships could be turned round. We think this is the first step. The controller, Mr. Vincent Macdonald, has the confidence of the longshoremen, the shipowners and the stevedoring companies. Then we brought a man from Vancouver who has had a great deal of experience in this line on the Pacific coast, and we also had a technical expert, Mr. Green, who organized this system of loading ships by lighter which is being used in the port of Halifax.
What is the name of the man from Vancouver?
Speaking from memory, Mr. Train.

From the employers
federation?

I would assume so. We have set up an advisory committee, representative of the union and the ship owners, to advise the controller. I think we have been as fair as we possibly can be. Naturally, when you discuss these matters with both employers and employees there is a lot of cross-questioning and some disagreement, but when the thing was finally settled the order in council was approved by the men,

War Appropriation-Naval Services
by the shipping federation and by the stevedoring company. After all is said and done, it is something new in this war. We are making a determined effort to turn round the ships that come into the port of Halifax more quickly than they have ever been turned round before.
If certain aspects of the policy do not work out well, we shall have to retrace our steps. But it is something entirely new in the dominion, and I feel-and I said this when I addressed the longshoremen-that it is in their own best interests and in the best interests of industry and of the country. When the thing gets into practical application there may be objections from one side or the other, but I feel sure that this advisory committee, representing both sides, will be able to advise the government of any changes which are necessary in the set-up for the purpose of increasing the tempo of turning round the ships entering the port of Halifax. Anyone who knows Halifax and shipping knows there has been some delay in turning round the ships as quickly as possible. I do not need to tell the members of this house of the tremendous losses of shipping at sea and of the necessity of expediting the loading and unloading of ships travelling the shipping lanes to the old country and other parts of the world in the firing line in order to transport the products of industry and agriculture of the north American continent to where they are vitally needed. .

There are certain parts of the minister's statement with which I am in agreement. The movement of the ships should be speeded up; nothing should be allowed to impede them; but the minister did not answer my question whether the men knew what they were agreeing to, and whether they knew they were submitting themselves to fine and imprisonment. If the minister will do me the honour to read the remarks which I made when introducing this subject this afternoon, he will see that I approached it from the point of view of interrogation because it seemed to me to be introducing an entirely new principle. The minister himself said that it is a new system but, by the same token, he said they had it in Vancouver-
No, I did not say that.

-and it seemed to me there was a little inconsistency there. But I may have misunderstood him. I take it that this is the first time in this country that this principle of compulsion with respect to labour has been introduced into our economy?
Not at all. It is in shipping, and always was. A man has to sign articles on joining a ship.

That is entirely different. A man signs his articles, goes on board ship and knows that he is amenable to the discipline on board ship. But this is not analogous to that, and the minister will not say so.
I do say so.

Then I shall have to differ with the minister, and we do not have very much time to argue it out before six o'clock. I do say this, that when this order in council came to my attention, having read a great many orders in council I decided that this was the introduction of a new principle in our war economy. The minister justified it on more than one ground. First of all he says that it is necessary that the ships which come in and go out of that harbour should be speeded up, and I agree with that. We must do everything to expedite the dispatch of these ships.
But the question I ask the minister, and which I asked before, is this: Is it necessary to resort to this kind of policy at this time at that port, did the men who he says agreed to the underlying principle of this order in council know in fact what they were agreeing to, and were the conditions in the port of Halifax such that it was necessary to resort to a policy of this kind? If the answer to all of these questions is in the affirmative, I have nothing more to say. The minister knows the facts; I do not. But this having come to my attention entitles me, I think, to bring it to the attention of parliament with a view to eliciting the information for which I now ask.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The hon. member for Lake Centre asked how many wooden ships were being built in Canada. There are 28 wooden ships of substantial size-I am speaking only of the larger type of ships, not about the smaller boats at all-being built in Canada for the Canadian navy, and in addition there are 24 wooden ships being built for the British navy. These are all wooden ships, minesweepers and of that general class.
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition asked about the expenditure at Saint John, and I gave him the main expenditure in respect of a fitting-out berth on the south side of the dockyard. There are some other expenditures which perhatps he would like to have. An administration building is to be

War Appropriation-Naval Services
built at a cost of some $25,000, barracks at a cost of $40,000, and a recreation building at a cost of $7,000.
In connection with training purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We have at Saint John some 169 naval personnel in addition to the divisional strength.
And not much in the way of facilities at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is right. We are also building a workshop and ordnance store combined at a cost of some $45,000, and then there are some odd amounts for fencing, roads, waters, sewers, and so forth. The main item is for the fitting-out berth at the south side of the dockyard. It is a very long berth; I am not sure whether it is seven or nine hundred feet long.
Will these works be built by public tender?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Again I must refer my hon. friend to the Minister of Munitions and Supply, who builds the works. I think it is the desire of that department to proceed by public tender as far as possible, but there are cases where that is rather difficult when the work has to be done in a hurry.
It is our policy to proceed by public tender if it is possible to get competitive tenders, but my hon. friend will understand that the construction industry is very busy-

Not so
busy in New Brunswick.

If it is not busy in New Brunswick I can assure my hon. friend that it will be done by public tender. But sometimes there is only one contractor available to do the work.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Crerar the house adjourned at six p.m.
Monday, May 11, 1942
